stateSemantics.validation: int rejects values less than -1 with AOOE(millisecondsDelay). TimeSpan converts (long)delay.get_TotalMilliseconds() with truncation toward zero, then rejects below -1 or above 4294967294 with AOOE(delay). Keep long internally; do not narrow large valid TimeSpan delays to int.
stateSemantics.fractionalExamples: -1 tick and -9999 ticks truncate to zero; -10000 through -19999 ticks truncate to -1; -20000 ticks reject. At upper range use tick-exact vectors around 4294967294 and 4294967295 milliseconds, including fractional offsets, and preserve double-to-long source conversion rather than substituting an arbitrary duration rule.
stateSemantics.selection: After validation and Java-carrier checks: requested token returns FromCanceled(token), even at zero; otherwise zero returns CompletedTask; otherwise create cancelable promise if CanBeCanceled, else noncancelable promise. Infinite -1 installs no timer; infinite noncancelable remains pending with no registration or timer.
stateSemantics.fromCanceled: Construct a distinct canceled Task with supplied token, no fault and no original OperationCanceledException payload. Await throws TaskCanceledException bound to this Task, token equality preserved even after source disposal. Nonrequested None/default/live/disposed-nonrequested tokens reject.
stateSemantics.linearization: Task's existing synchronized terminal transition is the sole winner. Payload writes precede volatile status publication; only one of timer success and cancellation wins. Loser never overwrites state or creates a fault. Await returns on success, or TCE with original Task/token on cancellation.
stateSemantics.dispatch: A private per-Task volatile/lock-safe delay async flag is initially false. Cancellation callback sets it before invoking complete(Canceled). Completion reads it at the dispatch decision and queues every pending callback when true; state publication itself is synchronous. Timer completion may inline the first pending continuation if false. A cancellation race may set the flag before timer dispatch even if timer wins; accept async timer dispatch then. Existing TCS/Run/ValueTask producers never set the flag, retaining first-inline/additional-queued behavior. Already-completed continuation registration remains asynchronous.
stateSemantics.disposedTokens: Use a token obtained before source disposal. Disposed nonrequested tokens remain nonrequested and CanBeCanceled; registration may be empty, finite delay still succeeds, infinite delay remains pending. Already-requested then disposed tokens still produce canceled tasks. Do not call get_Token on an already-disposed source as a surrogate for Delay behavior.
stateSemantics.contextBoundary: No custom scheduler or ExecutionContext capture parity claim. New timer threads, worker threads and delay-specific fallback workers must be daemon and disable inheritable-thread-local inheritance, including lazy creation paths. Do not silently change old Task queue behavior; give Delay a private dispatch executor if necessary. Native uses UnsafeRegister/context-free timers; the existing Register adaptation is valid only in the stated bounded default-context profile.

privateDesign.composition: Private nested DelayState owns a new Task, optional TimerHandle and CancellationTokenRegistration, plus a resource lock and cleanupRequested marker. Task remains final. Place helper implementations nested/private, or a package-private TaskDelaySupport.java only if size requires it. No public nested interfaces, setters, constructors or cancellation producer escapes.
interfaces: Private DelayTimer.schedule(long milliseconds, Runnable callback) -> idempotent TimerHandle.cancel()

Per-invocation registration function mapping token/callback to the actual CancellationTokenRegistration, production using token.Register(Action); the test function gates before/after the real registration and returns that real CTR, never subclasses the final carrier
Per-invocation asynchronous Executor for delay completion/continuations
Package-private test entry point accepting an immutable per-call infrastructure object, never a global mutable hook
privateDesign.productionTimer: ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor with remove-on-cancel enabled and one scheduler worker is acceptable only for expiry notification. Scheduled work hands off to independent cached daemon workers and returns immediately; no arbitrary user continuation executes on the scheduler worker. Use java.base only. Native source supports callback threadpool dispatch; there is no exact thread-count or latency equivalence claim.
privateDesign.rejection: Define a delay-specific rejected-executor fallback using a fresh noninheriting daemon worker, so neither cancellation nor timer scheduler executes user continuations inline on rejection. Preserve exactly-once completion/dispatch attempts. Catastrophic allocation failure is not a fabricated native fault mapping; retain raw failure and make cleanup best-effort in finally.
privateDesign.construction: Create DelayState before invoking scheduling; finite timer may call back before schedule returns. Publish returned handle under resource lock, then dispose it outside lock if cleanupRequested or Task already terminal. Register cancellation only for cancelable non-fastpath promises; callback may run synchronously before Register returns. Publish returned CTR with the same late-publication rule. If setup throws after acquiring a resource, detach and dispose acquired resources before rethrowing the setup failure; do not fabricate a faulted Task for runtime infrastructure failure.
privateDesign.cleanup: Winning timer calls completion first, then cleanup; winning cancellation completes then cleanup. Use finally around completion dispatch so unexpected dispatch failure cannot skip cleanup once terminal. Cleanup atomically marks cleanupRequested and detaches published handles under resource lock; outside all Delay/Task locks dispose registration then timer. Each late-published resource observes terminal/cleanupRequested and disposes itself outside the lock. Idempotent handle/CTR disposal permits duplicate paths safely. Record the winning attempt before continuation dispatch inside the Task terminal transition (a private per-attempt outcome holder, never a public callback). Only that winner owns completion-finally cleanup; terminal status alone is not proof this caller won. Late-publication disposal remains a separate constructor obligation. This distinguishes a loser from a winner whose dispatch subsequently throws.
privateDesign.lockOrder: Never wait in CTR.Dispose while holding Delay resource lock or Task lock. Never hold resource lock across scheduling, registration, completion or arbitrary callback invocation. Source Cancel already releases CTS lock before callbacks. Cancellation cleanup can dispose its own registration without waiting; external timer cleanup can wait for an in-flight cancellation callback only while owning no locks the callback needs.
privateDesign.completionBeforeCleanup: Terminal status can precede cleanup while an inline timer continuation blocks. Require eventual resource cleanup after that continuation is released, not eager cleanup at the first status observation. Late constructor publication may independently dispose its returned resource while the winning continuation is still running; both orders are source-permitted.
privateDesign.retention: Canceled scheduled futures are removed from the queue. Detach resource fields after cleanup. Keep the public Task from retaining a completed DelayState unnecessarily; callback closures may retain it only until timer work/registration is released. No forced-GC timing acceptance assertion.
